plan: Original literary narrative (CLD-P-ACT-R-000046): a teenager's summer in an aunt's hand-lettering sign shop. Genre chosen to balance the bank (literary narratives are 12 of 45 passages). Topic checked against every ACT Reading, SAT R&W, ACT English and ChatGPT verbal passage (no sign-painter passage). Ten questions with four aimed at hard inference (tone of a simile, an indirect reply, an ironic change of mind, a narrator's doubt about a character's motive). Difficulty provisional. Relabelled to the lower blind rating: R046-01 medium→easy, R046-02 hard→easy, R046-03 hard→easy, R046-05 medium→easy, R046-07 hard→medium, R046-08 hard→easy, R046-09 medium→easy, R046-10 medium→easy. The four items aimed at hard were all rated easy or medium by both solvers.

passages.title: Letters by Hand
passages.text:
The summer I turned sixteen, my mother arranged for me to work in my aunt Rosalind's shop, which she described to her friends as "a sign business" in the tone people use for a relative who has taken up the accordion. I expected to sweep floors. Instead, on the first morning, Rosalind handed me a brush with a chisel-shaped tip, a jar of black enamel, and a sheet of glass, and told me to paint the letter O until I hated it.

I did hate it, by noon. My O's sagged on one side or bulged on the other, and the paint pooled at the bottom of each stroke like water collecting in a footprint. Rosalind looked at each one without comment and then scraped the glass clean with a razor. When I asked how many more she wanted, she said, "That depends on the O."

Most of her customers, I learned, were not looking for anything she offered. A print shop across the highway could cut vinyl letters for a storefront in an afternoon, in any of four hundred typefaces, for less than she charged for a day of work. People came to Rosalind when a window had an unusual curve, or when an owner wanted the gold leaf that the print shop could not imitate, or, more often, when someone's grandfather had once had a sign painted and the family wanted the new one to look the way the old one had. She kept a box of photographs of those old signs, many of them by painters who had died before I was born, and she studied them the way other people read letters.

By the third week, my O's had stopped sagging. I was promoted to the rest of the alphabet and then, in August, to a real job: the name of a hardware store, to be painted on its front window in letters a foot high. I worked from Rosalind's chalk outline and did not breathe through the first R. When I finished, I stepped back to the curb and saw what I had not seen up close. The second R leaned a few degrees farther than the first, and the S was a hair too wide at the bottom.

I offered to scrape it off. Rosalind stood beside me for a long time, long enough that the owner came out to see what we were looking at. "Leave it," she said finally. "A machine would have made both R's the same. That's how people would know a machine made them." The owner, who had been frowning at the S, seemed to decide that he had been admiring it all along.

I have since come to doubt that she believed this entirely; she scraped her own mistakes off without a second look. But I think she understood something about the people who came to her shop that I did not yet understand. They were not paying for letters. They were paying to have someone stand on the sidewalk and look, for a long time, at the front of the place they had built. On the bus home that evening, I noticed the signs along the route for the first time—which ones had been cut and which had been painted—and I found that I could tell.

candidates.subskill: Main idea of a literary passage
candidates.stem: Which of the following best describes the main focus of the passage?

choices.A: A narrator explains how to paint letters on glass, step by step, for readers who want to learn the craft.
choices.B: A narrator describes a rivalry between an aunt's sign shop and a print shop across the highway.
choices.C: A narrator recalls a summer job in which an aunt's trade changed how the narrator sees handmade work.
choices.D: A narrator regrets having spoiled a store's window and losing a customer for an aunt's business.

candidates.evidence: I found that I could tell
candidates.explanation: The passage follows the narrator's summer in Rosalind's shop and ends with the narrator able to see the difference between painted and cut signs—a changed perception.

A.rationale: The passage includes some technique but centers on the narrator's experience and changing perception, not instructions.

B.rationale: The print shop is mentioned as context; there is no rivalry plot.

D.rationale: The owner ends up admiring the sign, and nothing suggests a lost customer.

hints: How is the narrator different at the end?

strategy.explanation: Summarize the beginning and the end, then choose the choice that covers both.

candidates.remember: A literary main idea usually tracks how a character changes.

candidates.stem: The narrator's description of how the mother referred to Rosalind's shop (paragraph 1) mainly suggests that the mother:

choices.A: was proud of her sister's success and liked to boast about the shop to her friends.
choices.B: regarded the business as an odd and somewhat unserious pursuit.
choices.C: did not really know what kind of work Rosalind's shop actually did each day.
choices.D: hoped that the narrator would someday take over the business from Rosalind.

candidates.evidence: in the tone people use for a relative who has taken up the accordion
candidates.explanation: The comparison to a relative who "has taken up the accordion" signals that the mother saw the shop as a quaint, not quite serious occupation.

A.rationale: Comparing the tone to that used for a relative who "has taken up the accordion" suggests mild embarrassment, not pride.

C.rationale: She names it correctly as "a sign business"; the point is her tone, not her knowledge.

D.rationale: Nothing in the passage indicates the mother's hopes for the narrator's career.

hints: What attitude does the accordion comparison convey?

strategy.explanation: Focus on the simile and the word "tone."

candidates.remember: Similes about tone reveal attitude; ask what feeling the comparison carries.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must interpret a humorous simile about tone rather than the literal words "a sign business."

candidates.stem: When Rosalind says, "That depends on the O" (paragraph 2), she most nearly means that:

choices.A: she has not yet decided which letter of the alphabet the narrator should practice next.
choices.B: the number of letters needed depends on the size of the sign that the shop is currently painting.
choices.C: some O's are much harder to paint than others because of differences in their size and shape.
choices.D: the narrator will keep practicing until the letters are acceptable, however long that takes.

candidates.evidence: When I asked how many more she wanted
candidates.explanation: Asked how many more O's to paint, Rosalind answers that it depends on the O—the narrator will stop when an O is good enough.

A.rationale: The answer concerns how many more O's to paint, not which letter comes next.

B.rationale: No particular sign is involved; the narrator is practicing on a sheet of glass.

C.rationale: She is not comparing different O's; she means the count depends on the quality of the narrator's work.

strategy.explanation: Reread the narrator's question just before the remark.

candidates.remember: Interpret a short reply by first identifying the question it answers.

author_checklist.hardness: The remark is indirect; students must connect it to the narrator's question and the scraped-off attempts.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, which of the following was a reason customers came to Rosalind instead of the print shop?

choices.A: They wanted gold leaf, which the print shop could not imitate.
choices.B: They needed their storefront signs finished in less than a single afternoon.
choices.C: They wanted to be able to choose from hundreds of different typefaces.
choices.D: They wanted to pay less for a sign than the print shop charged them.

candidates.evidence: the gold leaf that the print shop could not imitate
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists gold leaf, "which the print shop could not imitate," among the reasons people came to Rosalind.

B.rationale: The print shop, not Rosalind, could finish in an afternoon.

C.rationale: The print shop offered four hundred typefaces.

D.rationale: The print shop charged less than Rosalind did.

hints: Find the sentence that begins "People came to Rosalind when."

strategy.explanation: Scan paragraph 3 for the list of reasons.

candidates.remember: Check whether a detail belongs to the right person or business.

candidates.stem: In the passage, the detail that Rosalind "studied them the way other people read letters" (paragraph 3) mainly serves to suggest that she:

choices.A: treated the old signs as personal records worth close and careful attention.
choices.B: was trying to copy exactly the typefaces used by the painters who had died.
choices.C: preferred reading old letters to painting new signs for her customers.
choices.D: kept the photographs because she had painted many of the old signs herself.

candidates.evidence: she studied them the way other people read letters
candidates.explanation: Comparing her study of the photographs to reading letters suggests she approached them as personal, meaningful documents deserving careful attention.

B.rationale: The comparison stresses attention and feeling, not copying.

C.rationale: The comparison is figurative; it does not describe her reading habits.

D.rationale: The passage says many were by painters who had died before the narrator was born.

hints: What do people usually feel when they read letters?

strategy.explanation: Ask what the comparison adds about her attitude.

candidates.remember: A comparison's function is usually to reveal attitude or value.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, which of the following happened first?

choices.A: The narrator painted the name of a hardware store.
choices.B: The narrator was promoted to the rest of the alphabet.
choices.D: The narrator noticed the difference between cut and painted signs on the bus.

candidates.evidence: By the third week, my O's had stopped sagging.
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 says that by the third week the O's stopped sagging, after which the narrator moved on to the alphabet and then, in August, the hardware sign.

A.rationale: This came in August, after the narrator had moved on to the rest of the alphabet.

B.rationale: This came after the O's stopped sagging.

D.rationale: This happened on the evening the hardware sign was finished.

hints: Put the events in paragraph 4 in order.

strategy.explanation: Look for time markers like "By the third week" and "in August."

candidates.remember: Time words signal sequence; follow them in order.

candidates.stem: The statement that the owner "seemed to decide that he had been admiring it all along" (paragraph 5) most strongly suggests that the owner:

choices.A: had noticed the uneven letters on the window before Rosalind or the narrator did.
choices.B: changed his view of the S after hearing Rosalind's explanation.
choices.C: wanted the narrator to scrape off the whole sign and then repaint it carefully.
choices.D: had never looked closely at the new sign on his window until Rosalind spoke.

candidates.evidence: The owner, who had been frowning at the S
candidates.explanation: The owner was frowning at the S, but after Rosalind explained that uneven letters show handwork, he "seemed to decide that he had been admiring it all along"—a quiet, slightly comic change of mind.

A.rationale: He had been frowning at the S, but the sentence's point is that his view changed, not that he noticed first.

C.rationale: His change of mind points the other way: he came to admire the S.

D.rationale: He had been frowning at the S, so he had already looked at it closely.

hints: What was the owner doing before Rosalind spoke?

strategy.explanation: Compare "frowning at the S" with "admiring it all along."

candidates.remember: Irony often shows a character changing a view while pretending not to.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must read the irony of "admiring it all along" against the earlier frowning.

candidates.stem: In the last paragraph, the narrator's comment that Rosalind "scraped her own mistakes off without a second look" mainly serves to:

choices.A: suggest that her remark to the owner may have been partly a kindness rather than a fixed belief.
choices.B: prove that Rosalind never made mistakes in her own work.
choices.C: show that the narrator's letters were better than Rosalind's.
choices.D: explain why Rosalind eventually decided to scrape off the hardware sign.

candidates.evidence: she scraped her own mistakes off without a second look
candidates.explanation: Because Rosalind did not tolerate her own mistakes, the narrator doubts she fully believed that uneven letters were better; her remark to the owner may have been meant to protect the narrator's work.

B.rationale: Scraping off her mistakes shows she did make them.

C.rationale: The comment contrasts her standards for herself, not the quality of their work.

D.rationale: Rosalind told the narrator to leave the hardware sign.

hints: How does Rosalind treat her own mistakes, compared with what she told the owner?

strategy.explanation: Connect the comment to the narrator's stated doubt.

candidates.remember: When a narrator doubts a character's words, look for evidence of a different motive.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must infer an unstated motive by contrasting Rosalind's words with her own practice.

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 2, the word "pooled" most nearly means:
candidates.evidence: like water collecting in a footprint
candidates.explanation: The paint "pooled at the bottom of each stroke like water collecting in a footprint"—it gathered, or collected.

A.rationale: "Shared" is a common meaning of "pool," but paint collecting at the bottom of a stroke is not being shared.

B.rationale: The paint gathers in one place; nothing suggests it became thinner.

C.rationale: The comparison to water collecting in a footprint shows gathering, not drying.

hints: Use the comparison that follows the word.

strategy.explanation: Substitute each choice into the sentence.

candidates.remember: Context clues usually follow the word; test each choice in the sentence.

candidates.stem: The last sentence of the passage mainly indicates that by the end of the summer the narrator:

choices.A: had decided to become a professional sign painter like Rosalind someday.
choices.B: had learned to notice a difference that had been invisible to the narrator before.
choices.C: had come to prefer cut vinyl signs to the painted signs Rosalind made.
choices.D: felt embarrassed by the poorly made signs along the bus route home.

candidates.evidence: I noticed the signs along the route for the first time
candidates.explanation: The narrator notices the signs "for the first time" and finds that it is possible to tell painted from cut letters—a new way of seeing.

A.rationale: The passage does not say what career the narrator chose.

C.rationale: The passage does not state any preference; it says the narrator could tell them apart.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests embarrassment; the narrator simply notices and can distinguish them.

hints: What could the narrator do on the bus that was new?

strategy.explanation: Focus on "for the first time" and "I could tell."

candidates.remember: An ending often shows what a narrator has learned.
